title: Slide 1 · Integrated Machine Learning Capstone
question: Why can getting closer to Ava's score of 60 after a gradient update leave the class unsure about future students?
answer: Ava's score helped choose that update. Other students supply independent evidence about whether the changed rule generalizes.

title: Slide 2 · Write the question as a prediction task
question: Could you include a field called final_grade when predicting before the exam?
answer: Only information actually available at prediction time belongs in the input. A final grade computed using the exam score leaks the outcome.

title: Slide 3 · Freeze the data, split and evaluation rule
question: After seeing the four test scores, may you try several new models and present the best on those four as an independent result?
answer: Those scores would then help select the model. Treat the change as exploratory and reserve a fresh independent test set for a new evaluation.

title: Slide 4 · Set two reference points
question: Why should two students with different study histories receive the same baseline forecast?
answer: The baseline deliberately uses only the training mean. Beating it measures whether the features and fitted rule add predictive value on this split.

title: Slide 5 · Fit a line using only the training rows
question: What would happen to the slope calculation if every training student reported the same number of hours?
answer: Every centered hour value would be zero. The denominator would vanish, so the data could not identify a change in score per extra hour.

title: Slide 6 · Select on validation and lock the rule
question: If the constant had beaten both rules on validation, what should you have selected?
answer: Select the constant under the written rule. A richer model must earn its place by predicting held-out outcomes well.

title: Slide 7 · Measure the result on the four held-out students
question: Did the fitted line beat the baseline for every test student?
answer: Tay's line error is 7 versus the baseline's 5.5. An improvement in the average can coexist with an individual regression.

title: Slide 8 · Interpret a probability only under its assumptions
question: Does 0.5 at four hours mean that half of future four-hour students have been shown to reach 70?
answer: That fraction follows from the assumed Gaussian curve. Check observed frequencies in a larger held-out sample and evaluate the assumed spread.

title: Slide 9 · Report a failure and test the recording assumption
question: Can these two groups establish that studying longer causes larger prediction errors?
answer: Each group contains only two students. Study behavior was observed, and the groups may differ in other ways. Report the observed errors and test the pattern on fresh records.

title: Slide 10 · Write a claim someone else can check
question: A reviewer gets exactly your numbers but concludes that one more hour of study will raise anyone's score by five points. What should you revise?
answer: Make the interpretation explicit: five is the fitted slope on fictional training records. A causal effect would require evidence about what would happen if study hours actually changed.

title: Slide 11 · Carry out your capstone investigation
question: A classmate wants to verify your conclusion. Which parts of your submission should they check first?
answer: They should be able to reproduce the split, verify which rows influenced fitting and selection, recompute both MAEs from the same test table, and match a specific limitation to evidence in that table or in the stress test. Someone who reruns the notebook should recover the same results from a clean session.

title: Slide 13 · Defend your capstone
question: Which evidence would most directly strengthen the claim that the fitted line helps on future exams?
answer: Collect a larger independent cohort with the same prediction-time features, apply the frozen line and baseline, and compare errors on the same new students while checking performance across relevant conditions.

title: Office hours · Why does the final model use fewer inputs than Module 01?
question: Why does the final model use fewer inputs than Module 01?
answer: Module 01 introduced weights by hand using both hours and sets. This capstone fits a separate one-feature line from training outcomes and compares both models on the same validation cases. More features do not automatically improve prediction.

title: Office hours · Why include a probability exercise when the main metric is MAE?
question: Why include a probability exercise when the main metric is MAE?
answer: MAE evaluates a point estimate. A distribution answers a different question, such as how plausible a score of 70 is at three hours. Stating a spread makes that assumption visible and gives us something new to check.

title: Office hours · How would I reproduce the capstone independently?
question: How would I reproduce the capstone independently?
answer: Copy the named rows and split, start the notebook from its first cell, and compare your two validation predictions for the fitted line with 60 and 70. Then check the four test predictions individually before comparing aggregate errors.

title: Office hours · What could change if these were real students?
question: What could change if these were real students?
answer: The chosen records might underrepresent particular courses, schedules or testing conditions. A genuine evaluation would need an appropriate collection design, sufficiently sized independent cohorts, and a documented policy for any intended use.

title: Exercise 1
question: Use a novel student with 2.5 hours and 1 set. Predict using the frozen line, training mean and Module 01 rule. If the score is 64, which is closest?
answer: The line and constant both predict 62.5, each 1.5 points away. The original rule predicts 20 + 25 + 5 = 50, 14 points away.

title: Exercise 2
question: Build and defend a comparison for an in-class variant with new named records.
answer: Choose a pre-exam target, keep each student in one split, fit the constant and a feature-based model on training only, select by validation MAE and evaluate the frozen choice and baseline on common test records. Report split names, predictions and errors so another student can reproduce the comparison.

title: Exercise 3
question: A new blind test contains scores 63 at two hours and 72 at five hours. Compare the frozen line and constant.
answer: Line predictions 60 and 75 give errors 3 and 3, MAE 3. Constant errors 0.5 and 9.5 give MAE 5. This small independent check favors the line by 2 points.

title: Exercise 4
question: A team uses the test scores to select a different standard deviation for each student and reports excellent likelihood on those same scores. Identify the problem and repair the design.
answer: The test labels influenced the predictions being scored. Fit a spread on training or calibration data, freeze it, and evaluate the same likelihood or calibration criterion on unseen students.

title: Exercise 5
question: For Tay and Uma compute signed residuals. What does their mean hide?
answer: Tay gives 75 − 68 = +7. Uma gives 70 − 75 = −5. Their signed mean is +1, but their mean absolute error is 6. The mistakes point in opposite directions.

title: Exercise 6
question: Propose one improvement after seeing the four test rows and describe how to test it fairly.
answer: One proposal is to fit a two-feature model using both hours and completed sets. Fit on training, compare on validation, and use a new untouched test cohort because the existing test set helped motivate the change. Report errors for both the new model and the original frozen line.
